results.title: Make Strategic Project Decisions With Go No Go Checkpoints
results.content: Published Time: 2025-05-13 21:21:47 +0100 +0100 Make Strategic Project Decisions With Go No Go Checkpoints : Growing Scrum Masters Make Strategic Project Decisions With Go No Go Checkpoints #### No Go Decisions Go/no-go decisions are critical checkpoints where stakeholders evaluate whether to proceed with, modify, or halt a project, feature, or release based on predefined criteria and current circumstances. These binary decision points help teams make clear, objective choices about moving forward. * Provides structured decision-making framework * Reduces risk by establishing clear evaluation criteria * Enables quick, decisive action based on data and evidence * Prevents resource waste on non-viable initiatives * Creates accountability and transparency in decision-making * Aligns stakeholder expectations and commitment How it is Used in Agile Teams typically employ go/no-go decisions at key moments: * Sprint Reviews: Determining if deliverables meet acceptance criteria * Release Planning: Evaluating readiness for production deployment * Feature Development: Assessing whether to continue development or pivot * MVP Launch: Deciding if the minimum viable product is ready for market testing The decision criteria often include: * Treating it as a mere formality rather than a genuine evaluation * Using subjective rather than measurable criteria * Failing to involve all necessary stakeholders * Not having clear fallback plans for “no-go” scenarios * Rushing decisions due to pressure or deadlines * Ignoring warning signs to maintain momentum A team developing a mobile banking app has a go/no-go decision point before releasing a new payment feature. * Successful integration with payment gateway * Performance testing showing <2 second response time If any criterion isn’t met, it’s a “no-go” and the release is delayed until issues are resolved. © Copyright 2019 - 2025 John McFadyen.

results.title: Understanding Risk and the Go/No-Go Decision
results.content: ## Understanding Risk and the Go/No-Go Decision. Sometimes we cannot begin to understand what the pilot was thinking when he or she decided it was OK to go fly on a day when the condition of the aircraft, the weather or the pilot should have dictated that it was clearly NOT safe to fly. This decision is often easy to make if the pilot is fit for flying, the weather is good, the aircraft is airworthy and the “mission” is well within the pilot’s comfort zone. However, a thorough understanding of risk is critical to the safe completion of every flight. 3. **Risk Management –** The elimination or mitigation of hazards to acceptable levels of risk. Proper management of the risks associated with any flight is a process. There are good processes and many tools (such as checklists) available to pilots to help them evaluate and manage risk. Flight Instructors now teach how to effectively manage risk with emphasis upon good Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) and proper situational awareness – there will be more on ADM later in this article. Analysis of accidents makes it clear that oftentimes pilots involved in an accident either 1) did not understand the risks associated with a flight, 2) underestimated the risk or 3) their plans (if any) to mitigate that risk were inadequate. Had he fully understood the risk and hazards associated with this flight, I would hope that he would have opted not to fly that day. *Antidote:* The FARs (it is often said) are “written in blood,” i.e. what we have learned from other pilots’ mistakes in the past (and often their “blood,”) are written into the current regulations to hopefully prevent similar accidents in the future. There are NO old bold pilots.” One of the problems with a macho pilot is that he will attempt to do something because of his big ego and end up taking a risk that a more cautious pilot would not take. By understanding risk and how to use proper ADM to make good decisions (including the Go/No-Go) before and during flight, you can and will be a better and safer pilot.x. results.title: Running a Successful Software Pilot Project - Vinton AI Notetaker
results.content: # Running a Successful Software Pilot Project. Published On: November 28, 2024Categories: AI, Nativevideo, VintonBy Luca Benini. Running a Successful Software Pilot Project. An old boss of mine used to say, “We are not in the business of selling pilots. In other words, when running a pilot project for a new software purchase, it should always be aligned with the end goal of a new subscription customer and the pilot should only be there to validate what the subscription will do. Running a pilot project is a useful part of the buying process. But how do you run a pilot that’s not just “useful” but truly impactful? A software pilot is all about fit:. * For **prospective customers**, it’s understanding if the solution aligns with their business needs. Before the pilot even starts define what success looks like and align each individual area of impact with a business-related outcome, ideally one that’s a priority for the Client or their particular industry. There’s always debate about how long a pilot should last. Because short pilots encourage teams to use the product in earnest. In our experience, if you run a two week pilot project, people will focus on it and test/try it in the last week anyway. A month-long pilot can lose momentum, but two weeks keeps everyone focused and invested. Start with a quick survey or set of metrics to capture the “current state” before the pilot begins. For example, when piloting Vinton, we might ask:. Then, ask the same questions post-pilot to quantify the impact. A noticeable improvement not only validates the software but also helps build a strong business case for full deployment. Before and after metrics create a clear picture of the solution’s impact, building a case for full deployment. Pilots aren’t just about testing the solution; they’re about building momentum. A well-run pilot is a strategy for success. With clear goals, focused execution, and measurable results, you’ll go from “let’s see if this works” to “we can’t work without this” in no time! Build pilot projects into subscription contracts (with an opt-out after the pilot is over). Interested in trying out Vinton?
